passages.text:
**Abstract.** The Stieltjes measure of every integrable minimiser of the
zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure, zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has full support on $[0,1)$ and a smooth
density that is strictly positive on $(0,1)$. We reconstruct OpenAI's quantitative
argument, organised around two uses of one spatial-moment inequality.
On a positive constant interval, it makes the derivative of the gradient
second moment strictly convex, contradicting the endpoint conditions
imposed by minimality. The same curvature and the bounded gradient
also exclude terminal gaps. Full support then gives moment identities and
smoothness; a local constant replacement transfers the inequality to the minimiser and
forces its density to be positive. H.-B. Chen previously proved full support
and smooth nonnegative density. We isolate the fixed-time spatial moment
and the positive margin that survives local replacement, while importing its
shape comparisons and full polynomial identity. We also derive the scalar value
identity and explain its classical optimisation consequence. For the quantum approximate
optimization algorithm (QAOA), we identify the rooted energy of a finite Gaussian
observable and the separate circuit theorem that approximates it. A further
second-moment theorem gives a measured near-optimal configuration on the same
random instance, with the circuit word fixed before the number of spins grows.
passages.rationale: The main result and the second use remain source arguments under the pure zero-field SK and integrable-minimiser hypotheses. The reconstruction genre and Chen attribution are preserved. The revised closing sentence selects algorithmic consequences as an outlook, without claiming a new theorem or a density premise for the algorithms.

passages.text: [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1][ACZ] proved infinite support. This need not be full support: the measure $\sum_{k\geq1}2^{-k}\delta_{1-2^{-k}}$ has infinitely many atoms and many gaps. [H.-B. Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][Chen] subsequently proved full support and smooth nonnegative density. We follow OpenAI's quantitative proof of the support conclusion and its further strict-positivity result. The feature used twice is a lower bound valid throughout every positive constant interval of an admissible coefficient, without a minimising assumption. **Theorem 1 (full support; quantitative proof following [OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][FS]).** If $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimises $\mathcal P$, then $$ \operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1),\qquad \gamma(t_2)>\gamma(t_1)\quad(0\leq t_10$, with probability tending to one there are configurations $\sigma,\tau$ with $|R(\sigma,\tau)-\rho|<\delta$ and both energies at least $n(P_*-\eta)$. This follows from [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Proposition 1, equation (5)][ACZ], using the Gaussian normalisation above. Our purpose is to isolate the spatial moment common to the support and density arguments, explain why it needs an integrated estimate, and identify what survives the local-replacement limit. The conclusions and the quantitative method are those of the cited sources. The proof compares two demands on a gap with two support endpoints. Minimality forces $q$ to agree with time there, with endpoint slopes at most one. On a positive constant interval a quantitative estimate makes $q'$ strictly convex, so its integral is smaller than the interval's length. This contradicts the required change in $q$. After excluding all gaps, the identity $q'=1$ supplies the equation from which the same estimate will force $\gamma'>0$. A qualitative crossing criterion already suffices for a bounded gap. The density argument needs more: an estimate for a local constant replacement that need not minimise, at a time where $q''$ need not vanish, and a positive lower bound that survives the limit. The second aim, in §5, is to follow the support identities to a finite Gaussian observable whose rooted energy a QAOA circuit approximates, then identify the additional concentration input for a measured configuration. These optimisation consequences use full support; strict density positivity is a further analytic conclusion. Readers interested in optimisation may accept Theorem 1 and continue to §5. Sections 2–4 assume Itô calculus and martingale convergence; the circuit construction is a separate imported theorem. Omitted proofs are linked to *From Parisi full support to deterministic QAOA circuits: A long reasoning record*, the [companion edition of 26 October 2026](../long/reasoning-record.md); original-source citations remain beside the imported inputs.

For an admissible coefficient, $\Phi$ is even, convex and one-Lipschitz
in space. Its positive-order spatial derivatives are bounded and
continuous on each strip $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$, $T<1$; the PDE
holds almost everywhere in time. The compact-strip approximation
theorem justifies the following Itô calculations even when $\gamma$
has jumps (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS]). The control method
has antecedents in [Jagannath and Tobasco (2016)][JT] at positive
temperature and [Auffinger and Chen (2017), Theorem 2 and
Corollary 2][AC] at zero temperature; see also [Chen, Handschy and
Lerman (2018), Proposition 2 and Theorem 5][CHL].

Fix a minimiser. Itô's formula cancels the drift of $u(t,X_t)$:
$$
du(t,X_t)=a(t,X_t)\,dB_t,
\qquad q(0)=0,\qquad q'(t)=\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2].
$$
In particular $q'$ is continuous across coefficient jumps. Minimality
means that every allowed one-sided change has nonnegative first-order
cost. The one-sided variation formula gives the rate of change of the functional
when $\gamma$ is replaced by $\gamma+\varepsilon\eta$ as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$:
$$
D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta]
=\tfrac12\int_0^1\eta(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt,                 \tag{1}
$$
for every integrable direction $\eta$ for which
$\gamma+\varepsilon\eta\in\mathcal U$ for all sufficiently small
$\varepsilon\geq0$ (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.1][FS]). Earlier
zero-temperature variation and support identities appear in
[Chen, Handschy and Lerman (2018), Propositions 3–4][CHL].

Adding a unit atom at $s$ raises the cumulative function at every
$t\geq s$, so its direction is $\eta=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}$. The
first-order cost is therefore a tail integral:
$$
G(s):=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\geq0.
$$
Here $G(s)/2$ is the first-order cost of the added atom. Conversely,
let $\nu=\mu_\gamma|_K$ for a compact $K\subset[0,1)$.
For $0\leq\varepsilon\leq1$, the measure
$\mu_\gamma-\varepsilon\nu=(1-\varepsilon\mathbf1_K)\mu_\gamma$
is nonnegative, and its cumulative function is
$\gamma-\varepsilon\nu([0,\cdot])\in\mathcal U$. Minimality gives
$$
0\leq D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\nu([0,\cdot])]
=-\tfrac12\int_K G(s)\,d\mu_\gamma(s).
$$
The change of integration order is justified by $|q-t|\leq1$ and
$\mu_\gamma(K)<\infty$. Since $G\geq0$, it vanishes almost
everywhere for $\mu_\gamma$, and continuity makes it vanish on
$S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$. The variation removes a fraction of
all mass in $K$, not only atoms; no density or probability constraint is assumed.

At a support point $s>0$, $G$ has a minimum. Hence
$$
G'(s)=s-q(s)=0,\qquad G''(s)=1-q'(s)\geq0,
\quad\text{so}\quad q(s)=s,\quad q'(s)\leq1.       \tag{2}
$$
If $0\in S$, contact gives $G(0)=0$; independently, zero field
gives $q(0)=0$. Hence $G(h)=\tfrac12(1-q'(0))h^2+o(h^2)$; nonnegativity gives the
same slope bound at zero. These are the contact conditions of
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.2][FS].

passages.text: **Lemma 2 (constant-interval curvature; [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][FS]).** Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$, with its associated diffusion and moment $q$. If $\gamma=c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, called a plateau, then for $t\in I$ $$ q'''(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0 \quad\text{if }c>0. \tag{3} $$ If $c=0$, then $q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0$. Minimality is not a hypothesis of this lemma. Section 3 derives its moment polynomial and explains the integrated estimate imported from the source. **Proof of Theorem 1, assuming Lemma 2.** A complementary interval with two support endpoints admits two contact conditions; an initial interval without support at zero has coefficient zero. For terminal gaps, the bound $q\leq1$ replaces the missing right contact condition. Suppose $(\ell,r)$ is a support gap with endpoints in $S$ and $r<1$. The coefficient is a positive constant there: support at $\ell$ and absence of mass immediately to its right force $\mu_\gamma([0,\ell])>0$. Strict convexity of $q'$ and (2) give $$ q'(t)<\frac{r-t}{r-\ell}q'(\ell) +\frac{t-\ell}{r-\ell}q'(r)\leq1 \qquad(\ell0$, hence $q'(t)1$. Convexity then gives $q'(s)>q'(t)>1$ for $s>t$. Consequently $q(s)>t+(s-t)q'(t)>1$ for $s<1$ sufficiently close to one, contrary to $q\leq1$. Thus $q(t)[long §5, “A shorter qualitative exclusion”](../long/reasoning-record.md#qualitative-terminal-gap) gives the full endpoint discussion. The stronger boundary estimate $1-q(t)\geq C\sqrt{1-t}$ for arbitrary coefficients constant near one is proved in [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3][FS] and [long §5, terminal boundary estimate](../long/reasoning-record.md#terminal-gap); [Chen (2026), Proposition 4.5, equations (4.27)–(4.38)][Chen] gives the square-root asymptotic under the terminal-gap hypothesis. The zero-coefficient heat argument and late-step variation have antecedents in [Chen, Handschy and Lerman (2018), Theorem 6][CHL]. These cases exhaust the complement of the relatively closed set $S$. Consequently $S=[0,1)$, contact gives $q(t)=t$, and differentiation gives $\mathbb E a^2=1$, including the right-hand value at zero. Moreover, $\gamma(t_2)-\gamma(t_1)=\mu_\gamma((t_1,t_2])>0$. This proves Theorem 1 using the stated analytic inputs.

passages.text: Full support does not force pointwise positive density. For instance, $\gamma(t)=\int_0^t(s-\tfrac12)^2\,ds$ has full Stieltjes support but $\gamma'(\tfrac12)=0$: every interval of positive length has a positive integral, although the integrand vanishes at one point. The quantitative remainder in (5) rules this out for a minimiser. First, the identity $\mathbb E a^2=1$ expresses $\gamma$ as a quotient of continuous moments and then gives smoothness. Only afterwards do we apply the fixed-time spatial estimate to obtain $\gamma'>0$. **Corollary 4 (smooth positive density; [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 6.4][FS]).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1, $\gamma(0)=0$ and $\gamma\in C^\infty([0,1))$, with derivatives at zero taken from the right. Its Stieltjes measure is $\mu_\gamma(dt)=\gamma'(t)\,dt$, and $$ 2\gamma'(t)\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^3] \geq\frac{\gamma(t)^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0 \qquad(0[long §9.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#smooth-density-consequence). Now the two differentiated moments are $$ \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E b^2=\mathbb E[d^2-6\gamma ab^2], \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E a^3=\mathbb E[3ab^2-3\gamma a^4]. $$ For a smooth time coefficient, differentiating $q''=\mathbb E b^2-2\gamma\mathbb E a^3$ therefore gives $$ q^{(3)}+2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3 =\mathcal C_\gamma(t). \tag{9} $$ This identity displays the two uses of the same spatial moment. On a plateau, $\gamma'=0$ and $(v,w,z)=c(a,b,d)$ recover (4). For the now smooth minimiser, $q=t$, so $q^{(3)}=0$ and the left side is $2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3$. Proposition 3 supplies the lower bound for this spatial moment. Apply Proposition 3 to the now smooth minimiser. Strict increase and $\gamma(0)=0$ give $\gamma(t)>0$ for $t>0$; (9) therefore gives (7). Strictness follows from $\gamma(t)>0$ and $\mathbb E a^4\geq(\mathbb E a^2)^2=1$. In particular, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$ \mathbb E a^3\leq\sqrt{\mathbb E a^2\,\mathbb E a^4} =\sqrt{\mathbb E a^4}\leq\mathbb E a^4, $$ so the same inequality implies $\gamma'(t)\geq\gamma(t)^2/2000$ for $0[Long §§9.1–9.2](../long/reasoning-record.md#smooth-density-consequence) retain the smoothness argument and fixed-time transfer, including the common approximation bounds. **Earlier and related estimates.** The backward shape comparisons, transformed density and positive-temperature gap-crossing argument appear in [Lopatto (2026), v3, Propositions 3.6, 7.1 and 9.1][Lopatto]. [H.-B. Chen (2026), Proposition 4.2][Chen] proves the zero-temperature crossing implication $q''=0\Rightarrow q'''>0$ under the minimiser convention of §3.1. [Lopatto's v4, Proposition 5.1 and Corollary 5.6][Lopatto-v4] give qualitative crossing for arbitrary positive-temperature probability measures. In unit-noise coordinates, their cumulative coefficient is $\gamma_\beta=\beta\alpha_\nu$, where $\alpha_\nu(t)=\nu([0,t])$, and the terminal value is $\beta^{-1}\log\cosh(\beta x)$. Every bounded $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ has this form: choose $\beta>0$ with $\beta\geq\sup\gamma$ and put the remaining probability mass at one. Thus the coefficient classes alone do not distinguish the estimates; the terminal datum and the quantitative control through its zero-temperature limit matter. [Lopatto's external-field paper, Theorem 2.3 and §8][Lopatto-field] also uses a fixed-time spatial inequality for support and positive density. At a continuity point, monotonicity supplies its one-sided coefficient bounds; on a smooth full-support interval of the minimiser, its scalar conditions become equalities. Appendix B gives the positive-temperature, zero-field strict-density result. The bound used here instead applies at a nonstationary comparison time and retains an explicit fourth-moment margin through the local replacement with terminal datum $|x|$. The rescaling and exact hypothesis comparisons are in [long §2.3, finite-temperature dictionary](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-temperature-dictionary).

passages.text: ### 5.1 A martingale formula for the ground-state value The support identities give a scalar representation of $P_*$. Set $M_t=u(t,X_t)$, the bounded gradient martingale satisfying $dM_t=a(t,X_t)\,dB_t$. The quadratic variations distinguish the two Hessian moments: $$ d\langle M\rangle_t=a(t,X_t)^2\,dt, \qquad d\langle M,B\rangle_t=a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ Full support gives $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$, hence each increment $M_t-M_s$ has unconditional variance $t-s$. This normalises the discrete increments below. The first moment of $a$ instead gives covariance with the driving noise. Let $U$ be the almost-sure and $L^2$ limit of $M_t$. The value identity is $$ P_*=\mathbb E[UB_1] =\int_0^1\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)]\,dt. \tag{10} $$ Boundedness gives $|U|\leq1$, while $\mathbb E M_t^2\to1$ gives $\mathbb E U^2=1$; therefore $U^2=1$ almost surely. To see the cancellation behind (10), the terminal convergence of the convex value functions gives $UX_1=|X_1|$ (the equality is automatic on $X_1=0$), while Itô's formula gives $\mathcal P(\gamma)=\mathbb E|X_1|-\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt$. Multiplying $X_1=B_1+\int_0^1\gamma(t)M_t\,dt$ by $U$ cancels that integral because $\mathbb E[UM_t]=t$. The Parisi formula then gives (10). The endpoint limits and stochastic-integral covariance are proved in [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.1][FS] and the long record, [§6, “Recovering the value from a martingale”](../long/reasoning-record.md#scalar-value-identities). This argument uses full support, not the density corollary. In particular, convexity and Cauchy–Schwarz give $0\leq\mathbb E a\leq1$, so $$ 0\leq P_*-\int_0^T\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)]\,dt\leq1-T. $$ One can therefore fix the terminal cutoff before discretising the diffusion. The gradient-martingale and value methods have antecedents in [Montanari, preprint v2, Lemmas 3.2–3.4][Montanari], under its positive-temperature support assumption, and in the zero-temperature calculations of [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, preprint v1, Lemmas 6.5 and 6.13][EAMS]. [Sellke, preprint v4, Proposition 3.10 and Lemma 3.11, p. 17][Sellke] gives the closely related finite-cutoff cancellation by applying Itô's formula to $\Phi$ and $x\Phi_x$. ### 5.2 The classical algorithm Full support and existence give an attained, strictly increasing minimiser in the monotone zero-temperature class. This is Assumption 2 of [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, preprint v1][EAMS]. Their Corollary 2.2 then gives, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a randomised algorithm returning a configuration within $\varepsilon n$ of the finite SK maximum with probability tending to one over couplings and algorithmic randomness. Its cost is $C(\varepsilon)n^2$ real-arithmetic operations with the prescribed scalar functions and normalisers available; this includes no separate numerical-preprocessing or finite-precision bound. [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.3][FS] and [long §9.4](../long/reasoning-record.md#classical-algorithm-consequence) check the Gaussian convention and operation count. Chen already records the classical consequence in [§1, p. 4][Chen]. Their incremental approximate message-passing iterates use the coupling matrix. Their scalar description uses the martingale multiplier and state drift $$ u_{\rm EAMS}(t,x)=a(t,x),\qquad v_{\rm EAMS}(t,x)=\gamma(t)u(t,x). $$ Thus their noise multiplier is the Hessian, whereas our $u$ is the gradient. The bounded martingale $M_t$ and $\mathbb E a^2=1$ give the required variance normalisation. With the fixed-strip regularity and discretisation estimates, [their Theorem 2][EAMS] achieves energy arbitrarily close to the truncated first-moment integral in (10). Strict positivity of the density is unnecessary.

The EAMS consequence uses attained strict increase and the variance-normalized bounded martingale, retains additive error/probability/arithmetic-model qualifications, and credits Chen section1 p4 for the earlier explicit implication. passages.text: ### 5.3 A fixed QAOA circuit before the thermodynamic limit The remaining consequence uses a separate circuit approximation theorem, stated as Proposition 5 below. We give its finite Gaussian input and identify the energy it approximates. Its operator and control construction is developed in the companion; the support and density proofs above do not require those additional prerequisites. Let $\widehat Z_i,\widehat X_i$ be Pauli operators, and define the cost and mixer by $$ C_{n,J}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i0$ there is one finite $W$ with $v(W)\geq P_*-\varepsilon$, whose depth and angles depend on $\varepsilon$ but not on $n$ or $J$. The instance still determines $C_{n,J}$. Here depth counts global cost–mixer layers; their elementary gate counts depend on the implementation. This order of limits differs from the fixed-instance depth limit in [Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann, §VI][FGG], which permits instance-dependent choices. The common-circuit conclusion was conjectured by [Basso, Farhi, Marwaha, Villalonga and Zhou (2022), §7, equation (7.2)][BFMVZ]. **The finite Gaussian input.** Fix the minimiser and its diffusion, a cutoff $0[long §7, “A finite Gaussian spin and its adjacent correlations”](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-gaussian-approximation). **Proposition 5 (circuit approximation; a consequence of [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–5][Q]).** For each fixed $T,N$ in the preceding construction with finite positive normalisers, and every $\eta>0$, there is a finite ordinary QAOA word $W$, with deterministic angles independent of $n$ and $J$, such that $$ |v(W)-S_{T,N}|<\eta. $$ **Why the adjacent pairing is the energy.** We use the rooted Gaussian representation of [OpenAI (2026b), §2 and Lemma 3.1][Q], building on the spin–boson description of [Boulebnane et al. (2026)][spin-boson]. Its classical sector consists of square-integrable functions built recursively from a local Gaussian seed and child-generated Gaussian coordinates, with inner product given by expectation. For any finite list of fixed centred real child directions, their coordinates at the receiving root have a joint centred Gaussian law. For two such directions $f,g$, $$ \mathbb E[\mathsf G(f)\mathsf G(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle. $$ The directions are fixed elements of the child space, even when their values depend on the child's Gaussian coordinates. The receiving root's seed is independent of these coordinates; compatible embeddings preserve them as the recursive depth grows. The root shift $\mathsf L$ inserts a child direction into the first Gaussian chaos (the linear Gaussian part) with constant receiving-root state. Its adjoint projects onto that part and returns the child direction. The [one-pair calculation at the start of long §8](../long/reasoning-record.md#depth-one-calibration) checks this representation's energy against the finite SK circuit before the general construction in §8.1. Start with a standard normal receiving-root seed $g_0$ and recursively put $Z_{j+1}=\mathsf G(g_j)$. The orthonormal child directions give independent standard Gaussian lifts, reproducing the scalar law. The finite spin $F_N$ depends only on those lifts. Projection therefore gives the exact rooted-energy identity $$ \begin{aligned} \mathsf L^*F_N&=\sum_{j=0}^N\mathbb E[F_NZ_{j+1}]g_j,\\ \mathcal E(F_N):=\operatorname{Re}\langle F_N,\mathsf L F_N\rangle &=\sum_{j=0}^N\mathbb E[F_Ng_j]\,\mathbb E[F_NZ_{j+1}] =S_{T,N}. \end{aligned} \tag{12} $$ Independence of the receiving-root seed removes the $j=0$ term. This identity concerns the finite Gaussian formula in a limiting rooted space, not a finite-$n$ circuit. The unshifted pairing can have the same scalar limit without identifying this energy. The construction and projection are proved in [long §8.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#rooted-energy). The shift records the lift from a child direction $g_j$ to the receiving coordinate $Z_{j+1}$. A one-step example distinguishes it from the unshifted pairing. For the nonminimising heat coefficient $\gamma=0$, take $T=4/5$ and $N=1$. Then $g_1=Z_1$ and $F_1=\operatorname{sgn}(2Z_1+Z_2)$, so Gaussian regression gives $$ S_{T,1}=\frac4{5\pi},\qquad \mathbb E[F_1g_1]\,\mathbb E[F_1Z_1]=\frac8{5\pi}. $$ This tests the finite representation, not the minimiser-dependent limit in (11). The calculation is in [long §10.4, “An exact one-step calculation”](../long/reasoning-record.md#one-step-example). **Construction underlying Proposition 5.** [OpenAI (2026b), §§3–5][Q] smooths the spin and approximates every transmitted function by a bounded smooth map, preserving oddness; smoothing the final sign alone is insufficient. Its class exclusions prevent return through a traversed branch and reserve helper classes on which the output is zero, with positive probabilities fixed during synthesis. The resulting finite formula is approximated in energy using temporary Gaussian controls, with the same sitewise seeds throughout the word. Removing those controls produces an ordinary word, whose limiting energy is $v(W)$ by the fixed-word transfer. The approximation errors are absolute and can be chosen successively for each fixed $S_{T,N}$, before it is chosen close to $P_*$. The preserved quantity is energy; the measured-configuration conclusion below uses a further concentration theorem. The complete error bound is in [long §8.6, finite-formula energy approximation](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-formula-energy-error), with the constructions and their hypotheses in [long §§8.1–8.6](../long/reasoning-record.md#qaoa-construction). The deduction of near-optimality is now explicit: $$ P_*-v(W)\leq (P_*-I_T)+|I_T-S_{T,N}|+|S_{T,N}-v(W)|. \tag{13} $$ Choose $T$ so that $1-T<\varepsilon/3$, then $N$ so that the second term is below $\varepsilon/3$, and finally use Proposition 5 with $\eta<\varepsilon/3$. These finite choices give $v(W)>P_*-\varepsilon$ before $n$ tends to infinity. The source's Appendix A supplies an alternative positive-temperature input to the same synthesis. This construction supplies no bounds on depth or cost-angle magnitudes in terms of accuracy, and no efficient procedure for finding angles. A separate estimate for the expected energy of a specified word is described in [long §11.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#finite-size-comparison). Its threshold depends on the word's depth and cost angles. Without bounds on those parameters it gives no threshold in optimisation accuracy alone; it also supplies no rate for measurement concentration. **Corollary 6 (a measured configuration on the same instance).** For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite ordinary QAOA word $W_\varepsilon$, chosen independently of $n$ and $J$, such that one computational-basis measurement $\Sigma$ satisfies $$ \Pr_{J,\Sigma}\!\left\{ \max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)-H_{n,J}(\Sigma)\leq\varepsilon n \right\}\longrightarrow1 \qquad(n\to\infty). \tag{14} $$ **Proof.** For a fixed word, put $Y_n=H_{n,J}(\Sigma)/n$ and $K_n=\max_\sigma H_{n,J}(\sigma)/n$. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou, §4, equations (13)–(22)][FGGZ] prove $$ \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}Y_n\to v(W),\qquad \mathbb E_{J,\Sigma}Y_n^2\to v(W)^2. $$ The second moment is $\mathbb E_J\langle(C_{n,J}/n)^2\rangle$, so it includes measurement variance as well as disorder fluctuations. Thus $Y_n\to v(W)$ in joint $L^2$. Gaussian concentration of the maximum and its defining mean limit give $K_n\to P_*$ in probability. Choose $W$ with $P_*-v(W)<\varepsilon/3$. With probability tending to one, both $K_n-P_*<\varepsilon/3$ and $v(W)-Y_n<\varepsilon/3$, which proves (14). The two energies use the same $J$; no independence between them is needed. The companion's [§11.2, “What is averaged, and a fixed-word probability consequence”](../long/reasoning-record.md#fixed-word-probability) gives the concentration argument and its further probability consequences.

passages.text: This AI-assisted article reconstructs the cited analytic arguments. The integrated estimate (5), its shape hypotheses and compact-strip approximation are substantial imported inputs. OpenAI's retained [full-support formal statement][support-challenge] asserts the support and moment conclusions conditional on an admissible minimiser, and constructs its associated diffusion. A separate [scalar formal statement][value-challenge] covers value identities and finite Gaussian approximation, with minimiser and diffusion premises for those clauses. Its third clause identifies the ground-state and Parisi values from a minimiser, constructing the diffusion internally.
